q.t: Which of these marks the beginning of British history?
q.e: The people of the Iron Age made the first coins to be minted in Britain, some inscribed with the names of Iron Age kings. This marks the beginnings of British history.
o: The first coins minted in Britain, inscribed with the names of Iron Age kings
The Roman invasion led by the Emperor Claudius
The building of Stonehenge in Wiltshire
The arrival of the first farmers from south-east Europe

q.t: Julius Caesar led a Roman invasion of Britain in 55 BC. What was the result?
q.e: Julius Caesar led a Roman invasion of Britain in 55 BC. This was unsuccessful and for nearly 100 years Britain remained separate from the Roman Empire. In AD 43 the Emperor Claudius led the Roman army in a new invasion.
o: It was unsuccessful, and Britain stayed outside the Empire for nearly 100 years
Britain was occupied and Hadrian's Wall was built
The Iceni surrendered and Boudicca was killed
Almost all of Britain was occupied at once

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
Hadrian's Wall was built in the north of England to keep out the Vikings.
q.e: Areas of what is now Scotland were never conquered by the Romans, and the Emperor Hadrian built a wall in the north of England to keep out the Picts, the ancestors of the Scottish people. The Vikings did not arrive until AD 789.

q.t: Which TWO forts are named in the handbook as part of Hadrian's Wall?
q.e: Included in the wall were a number of forts. Parts of Hadrian's Wall, including the forts of Housesteads and Vindolanda, can still be seen. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: St Columba founded a monastery on the island of Iona, off the coast of what is now Scotland. St Augustine led missionaries from Rome and became the first Archbishop of Canterbury.
o: St Columba founded a monastery on the island of Iona
St Augustine founded a monastery on the island of Iona

q.t: In which year did the Roman army leave Britain?
q.e: The Roman army left Britain in AD 410 to defend other parts of the Roman Empire and never returned. The Romans had remained in Britain for 400 years.

q.t: The Vikings first visited Britain in AD 789. Why did they come?
q.e: The Vikings came from Denmark and Norway. They first visited Britain in AD 789 to raid coastal towns and take away goods and slaves. Later they began to stay and form their own communities.
o: To raid coastal towns and take away goods and slaves
To trade wool with the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms
To spread Christianity in the north of Britain
To escape religious persecution in Denmark

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
The Domesday Book recorded who owned the land and what animals they owned.
q.e: William sent people all over England to draw up lists of all the towns and villages. The people who lived there, who owned the land and what animals they owned were also listed. This was called the Domesday Book.

q.t: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?
q.e: The capital city of the UK is London. The capital city of Scotland is Edinburgh, the capital city of Wales is Cardiff, and the capital city of Northern Ireland is Belfast.

q.t: Which TWO of these are Crown dependencies rather than parts of the UK?
q.e: There are several islands which are closely linked with the UK but are not part of it: the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man. These have their own governments and are called 'Crown dependencies'.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: 'Great Britain' refers only to England, Scotland and Wales, not to Northern Ireland. The official name of the country is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
o: 'Great Britain' refers only to England, Scotland and Wales
'Great Britain' refers to England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland

q.t: According to the handbook, what proportion of the UK population lives in England?
q.e: The population is very unequally distributed over the four parts of the UK. England more or less consistently makes up 84% of the total population, Wales around 5%, Scotland just over 8% and Northern Ireland less than 3%.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
Northern Ireland and Scotland have their own banknotes, and shops throughout the UK are obliged to accept them.
q.e: Northern Ireland and Scotland have their own banknotes, which are valid everywhere in the UK. However, shops and businesses do not have to accept them.

q.t: Which country celebrates its patron saint's day on 1 March?
q.e: Each patron saint has a special day: 1 March St David's Day, Wales; 17 March St Patrick's Day, Northern Ireland; 23 April St George's Day, England; 30 November St Andrew's Day, Scotland.

q.t: Which TWO patron saints' days are official holidays?
q.e: Only Scotland and Northern Ireland have their patron saint's day as an official holiday, although in Scotland not all businesses and offices will close. St Patrick is the patron saint of Northern Ireland and St Andrew of Scotland.

q.t: Which festival is celebrated by both Hindus and Sikhs?
q.e: Diwali normally falls in October or November and lasts for five days. It is often called the Festival of Lights. It is celebrated by Hindus and Sikhs. There is a famous celebration of Diwali in Leicester.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: Eid al-Fitr celebrates the end of Ramadan, when Muslims have fasted for a month. Eid ul Adha remembers that the prophet Ibrahim was willing to sacrifice his son when God ordered him to.
o: Eid al-Fitr celebrates the end of Ramadan
Eid ul Adha celebrates the end of Ramadan

q.t: What is a constitution?
q.e: A constitution is a set of principles by which a country is governed. It includes all of the institutions that are responsible for running the country and how their power is kept in check. The constitution also includes laws and conventions.
o: A set of principles by which a country is governed
A written list of the rights of citizens only
The set of laws passed by Parliament each year
An agreement between the monarch and the Prime Minister

q.t: Why is the British constitution described as 'unwritten'?
q.e: The British constitution is not written down in any single document, and therefore it is described as 'unwritten'. This is mainly because the UK, unlike America or France, has never had a revolution which led permanently to a totally new system of government.
o: It is not written down in any single document
No part of it has ever been written down
It is written only in Latin
Only the monarch is permitted to read it

q.t: How is the Speaker of the House of Commons chosen?
q.e: Debates in the House of Commons are chaired by the Speaker. The Speaker is neutral and does not represent a political party, even though he or she is an MP. The Speaker is chosen by other MPs in a secret ballot.
o: By other MPs in a secret ballot
By the monarch on the advice of the cabinet
By the members of the House of Lords

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
Members of the House of Lords are elected by the people and represent a constituency.
q.e: Members of the House of Lords, known as peers, are not elected by the people and do not represent a constituency. Since 1958 the Prime Minister has had the power to nominate peers just for their own lifetime.

q.t: Which cabinet minister is responsible for crime, policing and immigration?
q.e: The Home Secretary is responsible for crime, policing and immigration. The Chancellor of the Exchequer is responsible for the economy and the Foreign Secretary for managing relationships with foreign countries.

q.t: Which of these is NOT one of the fundamental principles of British life listed in the handbook?
q.e: The fundamental principles of British life include democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs, and participation in community life. There is no place in British society for extremism or intolerance.

q.t: Which TWO things does the UK offer in return, according to the handbook?
q.e: In return, the UK offers freedom of belief and religion, freedom of speech, freedom from unfair discrimination, a right to a fair trial, and a right to join in the election of a government.
o: A right to a fair trial
